human_model: Root Cause Analysis in Incident Response
key_gap: Both sides converged on the same mechanism and the same five-item prevention/detection set (config-class approval + canary; restore 1%/delta alert; payments rotation; duplicate-rate metric; drift check; idempotency regression test), but the human separated trigger (C-4417) from root (auto-promotion heuristic classifying config as low-risk) from amplifier (retry storm) at first sight and ran two why-chains (failure AND detection), attributing the 42-minute MTTR to a routing/reorg gap. The AI named C-4417 as root in WHY and only promoted the pipeline to root during HOW's recurrence test; the detection root — the August alert-threshold raise, itself a small config change in the same class as the trigger — surfaced only in REVIEW. Correct conclusion reached by process, one stage behind the human's first pass.
learning_signal: For incident reviews, separate three objects before fixing: trigger (what changed), root (what class of change or process allowed it), amplifier (what multiplied it); a fix that kills only the trigger fails the recurrence test for the class. Run two independent why-chains — one for the failure, one for the detection failure (late page and long MTTR are separate gaps, each with its own root). Control changes (alert thresholds, promotion rules) are themselves config changes and deserve the same class lens as the trigger — 'the threshold raise is the same class as the incident' is the highest-leverage observation. Every shipped action item must carry an explicit recurrence test ('catches same-class incident: yes/no').
suggested_improvement: Add an incident-review template to the WHY stage: (a) build the evidence-tagged timeline before hypothesizing; (b) tag every hypothesis trigger / root / amplifier; (c) require a second why-chain on detection (why was it late? why was MTTR long?); (d) in HOW, gate every alternative on the recurrence test ('would this catch a same-class incident?'); (e) audit control changes (thresholds, promotion rules) with the same class lens as trigger changes; (f) ship ≤ 5 owned items, explicitly split prevention vs detection.

human_model: Root Cause Analysis in Incident Response
key_gap: The negative case validated the human model's registry weakness: strict pure RCA built the full timeline and three deep why-chains (descending into unfalsifiable org-culture territory: staffing, deadline culture, exec incentives) and generated twelve action items before touching production — restoring service 45 minutes later when the one-line fix plus restart takes 3. The AI classified the route as restore-first in META, capped WHY at the mechanism (invalid value via direct prod edit bypassing PR; watcher with no validation/rollback), shipped exactly two items each killing a distinct recurrence class, deferred three more with triggers, and restored in ~4 minutes. The AI's only residual gap: it flagged the deferred org-layer (why the PR was bypassed) but did not connect it to the positive-case lesson — both are the same 'small change, weak control' class — leaving the class generalization implicit.
learning_signal: RCA is gated by operational state: when production is degraded and the error log identifies the cause, restore first and cap the analysis at the mechanism level; deeper branches are admitted only with evidence tags, otherwise they go to a deferred list with triggers. Unverifiable org-culture chains are speculation, not causes. Shipped action items are bounded by recurrence classes: each kept item must kill a distinct class (direct prod edits; invalid config accepted), and a minimum-3 template is a sprawl trap, not a quality bar. The discipline from the positive case generalizes: 'what is the smallest class of change that produced this' — and control changes belong in that class.
suggested_improvement: Add an operational-gating rule to META/WHY: (a) before WHY, classify the route incident-vs-analysis; if production is degraded and evidence is unambiguous, flip to restore-first and mark WHY as capped-at-mechanism; (b) cap why-chains at the mechanism; deeper branches require evidence tags or are deferred with triggers; (c) enforce item-count discipline: every shipped action item must kill a distinct recurrence class, all else deferred; (d) after every incident, ask the class question ('smallest class of change that produced this') and audit that class including control changes (alert thresholds, promotion rules, config-edit paths).
